title: What's she like? — adjectives and comparison
goal: Describe people and things, compare them in two equally correct ways — and say which is the most.
bekal: form comparatives with the ending *-bb* and recognize the irregular ones

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ki az a Kati?
dialogs.intro: Anna is introducing her best friend to Budi tonight. Budi wants to know more first.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Ma este jön a barátnőm, Kati.
lines.id: My best friend Kati is coming tonight.
lines.literal: today evening she-comes the girlfriend-my, Kati.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Magas, barna hajú és nagyon vidám.
lines.literal: tall, brown haired and very cheerful.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.id: She's an architect. My best friend.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Milyen magas? Én elég alacsony vagyok.
lines.literal: how tall? I fairly short I-am.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Magasabb, mint te, de alacsonyabb, mint én.
lines.id: Taller than you, but shorter than me.
lines.literal: taller, than you, but shorter, than I.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Akkor nem baj. És beszél angolul?
lines.id: Then it's fine. And does she speak English?
lines.literal: then no problem. and she-speaks English-ly?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Jobban, mint én. Nagyon okos lány.
lines.id: Better than I do. A very clever girl.
lines.literal: better, than I. very clever girl.

notes: **Milyen ő? asks about character, not condition.** Compare *Hogy van?*, which asks how someone is doing. *Milyen* also works for things: *Milyen a lakás?* (what's the apartment like?), and as an exclamation: *Milyen szép!* (how beautiful!).

**Barna hajú** literally means "brown-haired". The ending *-ú / -ű* turns a noun into a "having-X" adjective: *kék szemű* (blue-eyed), *hosszú hajú* (long-haired), *jó kedvű* (good-humored). The pattern is very productive — and just like English "-ed" here, it instantly makes your descriptions sound grown-up.

**Idősebb nálad, or magasabb, mint te.** Two equally correct ways to say "than": the ending *-nál / -nél* on the thing compared, or the word *mint* followed by the plain form. The first is shorter, the second easier for beginners. Use either; both sound natural.
**Mint takes a comma.** Hungarian puts a comma before *mint* in comparisons: *magasabb, mint te*. It's a spelling rule Hungarians take seriously.

**Jobban, not jobb.** *Jobb* is the adjective (better), *jobban* is the adverb (better at doing something). Compare: *Ő jobb tanár* (she's a better teacher) versus *Ő jobban tanít* (she teaches better).

grammars.title: Comparison with -bb
body: One ending for all adjectives, with a linking vowel that follows vowel harmony.
after: Adjectives ending in a vowel just add *-bb*, with *a* and *e* lengthening as usual: *drága* → *drágább*, *olcsó* → *olcsóbb*.

**Irregular forms you must memorize**, because they're all used constantly: *jó* → **jobb** (better), *rossz* → **rosszabb**, *nagy* → **nagyobb**, *kicsi* → **kisebb**, *szép* → **szebb**, *sok* → **több** (more), *kevés* → **kevesebb**.
To sharpen the comparison, add *sokkal* (much more) or *egy kicsit* (a bit more): *sokkal jobb*, *egy kicsit drágább*.

grammars.title: Two ways to say "than"
body: Pick either; both are equally correct and equally common.

after: Note that the second way uses an ending you already know from unit 12, the "people and landmarks" group. Even the pronoun forms are the same: *nálam, nálad, nála, nálunk, nálatok, náluk*.
To say two things are equal, use *olyan … mint*: *Olyan magas, mint én* = "As tall as me". And for not equal: *Nem olyan magas, mint én*.

blocks.text: A subtlety worth noticing: Hungarians use *idős* for "old" when talking about people, and *öreg* feels blunter. For things, *régi* is used instead: *régi ház* (an old house), not *idős ház*.

blocks.title: The fastest way to lock in this table
items: Take five things around you and compare them in pairs out loud: *Ez a könyv nagyobb, mint az a könyv.* Then repeat the other way: *Ez a könyv nagyobb annál a könyvnél.*
Then compare yourself with three people you know. Sentences about people stick much better than sentences about things, because they're true.
